common_name: Penncross Creeping Bentgrass (Classic Golf Green and Fairway Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared, fertile seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Penncross is a synthetic variety combining three distinct creeping bentgrass clones bred at Pennsylvania State University.

directions: Penncross was bred at Pennsylvania State University by H. Burton Musser and released in the 1950s as a synthetic variety combining three distinct creeping bentgrass clones, giving it enough genetic diversity to avoid being wiped out by any single disease or stress event. For decades it set the industry standard for golf course putting greens, tees, and fairways across the northern tier of the country, valued for its fine texture, aggressive stoloniferous spread, and quick recovery from divots and ball marks. Establish only from seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed, since Penncross has no meaningful tolerance for casual lawn-type management and demands frequent, closely monitored mowing, irrigation, and fertility inputs to perform well. Newer cultivars have since surpassed it in disease resistance and uniformity, but Penncross remains widely planted and is still used as a benchmark in university variety trials.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Penneagle Creeping Bentgrass (Penn State Fairway and Green Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared, fertile seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Penneagle followed Penncross out of the Pennsylvania State University bentgrass breeding program.

directions: Penneagle followed Penncross out of the Pennsylvania State University turfgrass breeding program, selected for a more upright growth habit and improved resistance to dollar spot and other common bentgrass diseases. It has been used on both putting greens and fairways, since its slightly coarser, more vertical growth tolerates a modestly higher range of mowing heights than greens-only selections while still producing a dense, fine-textured playing surface. Establish from seed into a firm, well-prepared bed and budget for the same intensive mowing, irrigation, and fertility program that every creeping bentgrass cultivar requires to perform well. Like other older bentgrass releases it has gradually been supplanted on new construction by more disease-resistant modern cultivars, though it remains in service on many established courses.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: PennLinks Creeping Bentgrass (Penn State Improved-Density Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared, fertile seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; PennLinks is a Penn State release bred as an improvement on Penncross for finer texture and density.

directions: PennLinks came out of the bentgrass breeding work at Pennsylvania State University as an improvement on Penncross, selected for finer leaf texture, higher shoot density, and faster recovery from ball marks and foot traffic. It became a widely planted putting green and tee cultivar valued for producing a smoother, more consistent playing surface than older bentgrass releases at comparably low mowing heights. Establish from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed and budget for the same intensive mowing, irrigation, and fertility program every creeping bentgrass selection requires on managed turf. It tolerates close mowing well but has only modest resistance to some of the diseases that newer cultivars have since been bred to resist.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Penn A-4 Creeping Bentgrass (Penn State Ultra-Fine Low-Mowing Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a meticulously prepared, firm seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Penn A-4 belongs to Penn State's 'A and G' series bred for tolerance of extremely low putting green mowing heights.

directions: Penn A-4 is part of the 'A and G' series developed by Pennsylvania State University's turfgrass breeding program specifically for the extremely low mowing heights used on modern putting greens, well below what older cultivars like Penncross can tolerate without thinning. Its very fine leaf texture and dense, upright growth produce a smooth, fast putting surface, but that same fine, shallow-rooted growth habit makes it less forgiving of lapses in irrigation, fertility, or pest management than coarser bentgrass selections. Establish only from seed on a meticulously prepared, firm seedbed and expect to commit to a disciplined, closely monitored maintenance program indefinitely once it is grown in. It is intended for golf greens and comparable high-end putting surfaces rather than home lawns or general landscape use.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Penn G-2 Creeping Bentgrass (Penn State Fine-Textured Fairway and Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Penn G-2 is a sibling release in Penn State's 'A and G' creeping bentgrass series.

directions: Penn G-2 is a sibling release in Pennsylvania State University's 'A and G' creeping bentgrass series, bred alongside the A-series selections for fine texture and tolerance of very low mowing but marketed more toward fairway and tee use in addition to greens. It forms a dense, uniform, fine-bladed canopy that holds up well under the close, frequent mowing golf turf requires, while needing the same rigorous irrigation and fertility program as other modern bentgrass cultivars to avoid thinning. Establish from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed, and expect a longer and more carefully managed grow-in period than coarser-textured turfgrasses. As with other high-end bentgrass selections, it is suited to intensively managed golf and sports turf rather than casual home lawn use.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: L-93 Creeping Bentgrass (Rutgers Dollar Spot-Resistant Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; L-93 was selected through the Rutgers University creeping bentgrass breeding program for improved dollar spot resistance.

directions: L-93 was selected through the Rutgers University creeping bentgrass breeding program led by Reed Funk and became one of the most widely planted putting green cultivars on the strength of notably better dollar spot resistance than older releases like Penncross. It produces a dense, fine-textured, upright canopy that tolerates very low mowing heights while recovering quickly from traffic and ball marks, and it has repeatedly ranked among the top performers in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program putting green trials. Establish only from seed on a firm, finely prepared bed, and maintain the same intensive mowing, irrigation, and fertility regime that all greens-type bentgrass cultivars require. Reduced dollar spot pressure can lower fungicide inputs somewhat compared with older cultivars, but it is still a high-maintenance turf suited to golf courses rather than home lawns.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Declaration Creeping Bentgrass (Rutgers Disease-Resistant Modern Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Declaration is a Rutgers University release selected for improved dollar spot resistance and winter color.

directions: Declaration is a more recent release from the Rutgers University creeping bentgrass breeding program, selected for improved dollar spot resistance and better winter color retention than older industry-standard cultivars such as L-93. It forms a dense, fine-textured putting surface that tolerates very low mowing heights and has performed competitively in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials for overall turf quality. Establish only from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed and commit to the same rigorous mowing, irrigation, and fertility program every modern greens-type bentgrass cultivar demands. Its improved disease resistance can ease fungicide pressure somewhat, but it remains a specialized golf turf grass rather than a home lawn option.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Crenshaw Creeping Bentgrass (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Southern Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Crenshaw was released by the Texas A&M University turfgrass breeding program for better heat tolerance than older northern-bred bentgrass cultivars.

directions: Crenshaw was released by the Texas A&M University turfgrass breeding program and was notable for extending reliable creeping bentgrass putting green performance further into the heat and humidity of the southern transition zone than older cultivars could tolerate. It forms a fine-textured, dense canopy suited to low mowing heights, with better summer heat tolerance than many northern-bred bentgrass selections, though it still needs the same intensive irrigation and fertility management every greens-type bentgrass requires. Establish only from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed, and expect a demanding, closely monitored maintenance program through the heat of summer. It remains best suited to golf greens and comparable high-end putting surfaces rather than home lawns.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: T-1 Creeping Bentgrass (Heat-Tolerant Southern Putting Green Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; T-1 is a proprietary creeping bentgrass selection noted for heat tolerance in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials across the southeastern United States.

directions: T-1 is a proprietary creeping bentgrass selection that gained a strong following on golf courses across the southeastern United States and transition zone for its ability to hold up through summer heat and humidity better than many older bentgrass cultivars. It produces a dense, fine-textured canopy that tolerates very low putting green mowing heights and has placed competitively in National Turfgrass Evaluation Program trials for heat and disease tolerance. Establish only from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed, and maintain the same intensive irrigation, mowing, and fertility program every greens-type bentgrass requires, since heat tolerance reduces but does not eliminate the need for careful summer management. It is intended for golf greens and comparable managed turf rather than home lawn use.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: Seaside Creeping Bentgrass (Historic Pacific Coast Common Putting Green Grass)

planting.note: Seed into a firm, finely prepared seedbed in early fall, or spring as a secondary option; Seaside is one of the oldest named creeping bentgrass seed sources, originally harvested from stands naturalized along the Pacific coast.

directions: Seaside is one of the oldest named creeping bentgrass sources used in American golf course turf, originally harvested from stands of bentgrass naturalized along the Oregon and Washington coast long before modern plant breeding produced purpose-bred cultivars. It was widely used to establish golf greens and fairways in the early-to-mid twentieth century, valued simply for being a reliable, regionally available seed source rather than for any single standout trait, and it has long served as a reference 'common' entry in turfgrass variety trials. It forms a fine, dense, stoloniferous turf under close mowing but lacks the targeted disease resistance and uniformity bred into later Penn State and Rutgers releases. Establish from seed into a firm, finely prepared bed and expect the same intensive mowing, irrigation, and fertility demands shared by all creeping bentgrass turf.
sources: United States Golf Association Green Section

common_name: 4th Millennium Tall Fescue (Improved Turf-Type Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in late summer to early fall, or in early spring; 4th Millennium continues the 'Millennium' series of turf-type tall fescues following the earlier 2nd Millennium release.

directions: 4th Millennium continues the 'Millennium' series of turf-type tall fescues, following the earlier 2nd Millennium release with further refinements in leaf texture, color, and density aimed at modern home lawn and sports turf use. Like its siblings it keeps tall fescue's deep, drought-tolerant root system while offering a darker green color and finer blade width than older pasture-derived tall fescue types such as Kentucky 31. Seed into a firm, fertile bed in late summer to early fall for the best rooting before winter, or seed again in early spring if fall planting isn't possible. As a bunch-type grass it depends on overseeding rather than lateral spread to repair thin or damaged areas, and it performs best mowed at a moderate-to-tall height that helps it compete with weeds and shade out crabgrass.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Tall Fescue Variety Trials
University of Missouri Extension — Turf-Type Tall Fescue Lawns

common_name: Fiesta 4 Perennial Ryegrass (Improved Turf-Type Overseeding and Lawn Cultivar)

planting.note: Seed at 6-8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in early fall or spring; Fiesta 4 is the latest generation in the long-running Fiesta line of turf-type perennial ryegrasses.

directions: Fiesta 4 is the latest in a long-running line of turf-type perennial ryegrasses tracing back to the original Fiesta release, refined over successive generations for finer leaf texture, darker green color, and improved resistance to common ryegrass diseases such as gray leaf spot and red thread. It keeps the Fiesta line's hallmark of germinating and forming a mowable, wear-tolerant stand faster than almost any other cool-season turfgrass, which has made the series a long-standing choice for overseeding dormant warm-season lawns and athletic fields as well as year-round use in cooler climates. Seed into a firm, well-prepared bed in early fall or spring, and expect quick establishment but only modest ability to recover from bare patches since it is a bunch-type grass that fills in by tillering rather than lateral spread. It tolerates full sun to light shade and wears well under foot traffic, making it a popular blend component with Kentucky bluegrass and fine fescue for high-traffic lawns.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Perennial Ryegrass Variety Trials
